questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a research question from a broad topic
questions.stem: A manager asks the team to study workplace burnout and report findings by Friday

options.text: The topic names the subject and the question states what is being tested
The research question is the deadline while the topic is the report format
The topic is workplace burnout while the question asks whether remote work increases it
options.misconception: confuses the topic with the research question

options.text: The topic and question are interchangeable labels in a workplace report
options.misconception: treats topic and question as the same thing

questions.explanation: A topic names the subject matter, while a research question states the specific relationship or effect being investigated. Confusing the two leads to vague reports.
questions.hint: Ask what is being measured or compared.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Tell a hypothesis from a research question
questions.stem: The report states remote workers show higher burnout scores than office workers

options.text: The statement is a hypothesis because it predicts a direction of difference
options.misconception: labels a finding as a prediction

options.text: The statement is an observed result rather than a prior prediction
The statement is a research question because it compares two groups
options.misconception: confuses a comparison with a question

options.text: The statement is both a hypothesis and a conclusion at once

questions.explanation: A hypothesis is stated before data collection and predicts an outcome, while this sentence reports an observed comparison. Treating results as predictions reverses the logic.
questions.hint: Check whether the data already exist.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A consultant claims remote work always harms wellbeing in every workplace

options.text: The claim is falsifiable because harm is easy to measure
The claim cannot be tested because it is too broad to study
The claim is falsifiable because wellbeing is a clear construct
The claim is not falsifiable because always and every allow no counterexample

questions.explanation: A claim using always and every cannot be disproved by any single counterexample, so it is not falsifiable. Narrowing it to a testable scope would fix the problem.
questions.hint: Look for words that forbid any exception.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A report defines burnout as a score of 27 or higher on a 30-item scale
questions.explanation: The operational definition states the exact measurement rule used to classify burnout. Without such a rule the construct stays ambiguous.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Name the independent and dependent variables

stimulus.body: The HR report compares two offices. One office switched to flexible hours while the other kept fixed hours. Absenteeism was recorded for six months.

questions.stem: Which variable is the independent variable in this workplace report

options.text: Flexible versus fixed hours because it is the condition being compared
Office location because the two sites differ
options.misconception: treats a grouping label as the predictor

options.text: Absenteeism because it is the outcome the report tracks
Six months because it is the time span of the report

questions.explanation: The independent variable is the condition the researcher manipulates or compares, here flexible versus fixed hours. Absenteeism is the dependent outcome.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Remote workers in the report also have longer commutes saved and different job types

options.text: Report month is a confound because data collection takes time
Commute savings is a confound because it is an outcome
options.misconception: confuses a mediator with a confound

options.text: Absenteeism is a confound because it is measured later
options.misconception: mistakes a dependent variable for a confound

options.text: Job type is a confound because it covaries with remote status

questions.explanation: A confound varies with the predictor and can explain the outcome, so job type qualifies. Commute savings may mediate rather than confound the effect.
questions.hint: Ask what else differs between groups.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of a control condition
questions.stem: A workplace trial adds a control group that keeps the old process unchanged

options.text: The control group receives a placebo version of the new process
The control group provides a baseline for comparing the new process
The control group is excluded from all analysis
The control group exists only to balance sample sizes

questions.explanation: A control condition holds conditions constant so the effect of the change can be isolated. It is not merely a placebo or a size balancer.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Staff are randomly assigned to the new training or the usual training

options.text: Random assignment only matters for large organisations
Random assignment guarantees identical groups in every sample
Random assignment removes the need for a control group
Random assignment balances confounds across groups on average

questions.explanation: Random assignment tends to distribute confounding variables evenly across groups, supporting causal claims. It does not guarantee identical groups.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain placebo effects in a workplace study
questions.stem: Employees told a new policy will boost morale report higher morale scores

options.text: The improvement proves the policy works regardless of belief
The improvement may reflect expectation rather than the policy itself
The improvement is a measurement error to be discarded
The improvement shows morale is unreliable as a construct

questions.explanation: Expectations can produce changes independent of the intervention, creating a placebo effect. Blinding helps separate true effects from expectations.
questions.hint: Consider what belief alone can do.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: In a workplace wellness trial the assessor knows which group each employee is in

options.text: Only participants need blinding in any trial
Assessor knowledge has no effect on objective measures
Assessor knowledge can bias outcome ratings
Blinding is impossible once outcomes are self-reported

questions.explanation: When assessors know group assignment they may rate outcomes differently, introducing bias. Blinding assessors protects measurement validity.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A staff survey reports 62 percent satisfaction plus or minus 4 percent

options.text: The margin guarantees the true value is 62 percent
The margin means exactly 62 percent of staff are satisfied
The margin reflects the number of non-respondents
The true population value likely lies within 58 to 66 percent

questions.explanation: The margin of error defines a range around the estimate within which the true value likely falls. It does not make the point estimate exact.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Different samples from the same staff list yield slightly different means

options.text: The variation proves the staff list is inaccurate
options.misconception: blames the frame for sampling error

options.text: The variation is sampling error from using a subset
The variation means the survey is invalid
The variation is caused by careless data entry

questions.explanation: Sampling error arises because a sample rather than the whole population is measured. It is expected and quantifiable, not a flaw in the list.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Only 30 percent of invited staff completed the workplace survey

options.text: A low response rate proves staff are dissatisfied
A low response rate always invalidates the survey
A low response rate raises risk of nonresponse bias
A low response rate is harmless if the sample is random

questions.explanation: Low response rates increase the chance that respondents differ from non-respondents, creating nonresponse bias. It does not automatically invalidate results.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: The analyst divides staff by department and samples within each department

options.text: This is quota sampling because departments set targets
This is cluster sampling because departments are groups
This is simple random sampling because selection is random
This is stratified sampling because subgroups are sampled separately

questions.explanation: Stratified sampling divides the population into strata and samples within each, improving representation. It differs from cluster sampling where whole groups are selected.
questions.hint: Are subgroups fully sampled or selected as units?

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: The analyst randomly selects four offices and surveys everyone in them

options.text: This is stratified sampling because offices are subgroups
This is cluster sampling because whole groups are selected
This is simple random sampling of individuals
This is convenience sampling because offices are nearby

questions.explanation: Cluster sampling selects entire groups, or clusters, and includes all members. It is efficient but can increase sampling error.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Two coders independently rate the same interview transcripts

options.text: Inter-rater reliability measures internal consistency
Inter-rater reliability measures test stability over time
Inter-rater reliability measures agreement between coders
Inter-rater reliability is only for quantitative scores

questions.explanation: Inter-rater reliability quantifies how consistently different raters apply a coding scheme. Low agreement signals ambiguous criteria.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Margin of error and sample size
questions.learningObjective: Relate margin of error to sample size
questions.stem: A report uses a sample of 100 staff and reports a margin of error near 10 percent
questions.explanation: With 100 respondents the margin of error is roughly one over the square root of n, about 10 percent. Larger samples shrink the margin.
questions.hint: One over square root of n.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Most staff score near the maximum on a satisfaction scale

options.text: A ceiling effect is caused by random error
A ceiling effect means the scale is too long
A ceiling effect indicates high reliability
A ceiling effect limits detection of further improvement

questions.explanation: When scores cluster at the top, the measure cannot capture improvement beyond that point. This restricts variance and power.
questions.hint: What happens at the top of the scale?

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Plan sample size from an effect size
questions.stem: A planner increases the expected effect size in the sample size calculation

options.text: Larger expected effects require larger samples
Larger expected effects require smaller samples for the same power
Effect size does not affect required sample size
Effect size only matters for qualitative work

questions.explanation: Bigger effects are easier to detect, so fewer participants are needed to achieve the same statistical power. Smaller effects demand larger samples.
questions.hint: Easier to detect means fewer needed.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: The HR list of all employees serves as the sampling frame for the survey

options.text: The frame is the questionnaire used in the survey
The frame is the final set of survey respondents
The frame is the list from which the sample is drawn
The frame is the population parameter being estimated

questions.explanation: A sampling frame is the operational list of units from which a sample is selected. It is not the sample or the instrument.
questions.hint: Where do you draw names from?

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A report must reach remote staff in many small offices with limited budget

options.text: Convenience sampling is the only affordable option
Stratified sampling is always cheaper than cluster sampling
Simple random sampling guarantees the lowest cost
Cluster sampling may be cheaper but less precise than stratified

questions.explanation: Cluster sampling reduces travel and logistics costs by grouping respondents, but it often increases sampling error compared with stratified sampling.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a cost of cluster sampling
questions.stem: A cluster design surveys everyone in selected branches

options.text: Cluster sampling always reduces total cost to zero
Within-cluster similarity can inflate sampling error
Clusters eliminate the need for a sampling frame
Clusters guarantee representativeness automatically

questions.explanation: When members of a cluster are similar, fewer independent observations are gained, increasing sampling error. Cost savings must be weighed against precision.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Non-respondents to the staff survey are more likely to be remote workers

options.text: Nonresponse proves the survey is invalid
Nonresponse only affects the sample size
Estimates for remote-related outcomes may be biased
Nonresponse can be fixed by larger margins of error

questions.explanation: When non-respondents differ systematically from respondents on the topic, estimates become biased. Adjusting margins of error does not remove this bias.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Judge when a low response rate is problematic
questions.stem: A report with a 25 percent response rate still matches known staff demographics

options.text: A low rate is harmless whenever demographics match
Demographic match guarantees no nonresponse bias
A 25 percent rate is always unacceptable regardless of checks
Demographic match reduces but does not remove nonresponse risk

questions.explanation: Matching demographics on observed traits helps but cannot rule out bias on unmeasured traits. Caution remains warranted.
questions.hint: Observed traits are not all traits.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Classify a variable's level of measurement
questions.stem: Staff are asked to rank their satisfaction as low, medium or high

options.text: The variable is nominal because categories are labels
The variable is ordinal because order matters but gaps are unequal
The variable is interval because gaps are equal
The variable is ratio because a zero means none

questions.explanation: Ranked categories with meaningful order but unknown gaps are ordinal. Treating them as interval assumes equal spacing that may not hold.
questions.hint: Does order matter and are gaps equal?

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A workplace test gives consistent scores but measures the wrong skill

options.text: The test is both reliable and valid
The test is valid but not reliable
The test is reliable but not valid
The test is neither reliable nor valid

questions.explanation: Reliability is consistency of measurement, while validity is whether the right construct is measured. A test can be consistent yet measure the wrong thing.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A new hiring test score correlates strongly with later job performance

options.text: This proves the test is perfectly reliable
This supports content validity of the test items
This supports construct validity of the trait
This supports criterion validity against a future outcome

questions.explanation: Criterion validity is shown when test scores relate to an external criterion such as later performance. It does not by itself establish reliability.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A resilience scale correlates with stress coping and not with unrelated traits

options.text: This pattern supports criterion validity only
This pattern supports construct validity of the scale
This pattern proves the scale is perfectly reliable
This pattern shows the scale has no measurement error

questions.explanation: Construct validity is supported when a measure relates to theoretically linked traits and not to unrelated ones. It is a pattern of evidence, not a single correlation.
questions.hint: Look for convergent and discriminant evidence.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: The same staff complete a morale survey twice two weeks apart

options.text: Stability means the construct never changes
Stability across time proves the survey is valid
Stability of scores across time indicates test-retest reliability
Stability is irrelevant for attitude measures

questions.explanation: Test-retest reliability assesses score stability over time when the construct is expected to be stable. It does not establish validity.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A survey item asks about both pay satisfaction and workload in one question

options.text: The item only affects reliability, not validity
The item is fine because both topics are related
The item improves efficiency by combining topics
The item is confounded because two constructs are mixed

questions.explanation: Double-barrelled items combine distinct constructs, making responses uninterpretable. Each item should address one construct.
questions.hint: How many things are being asked?

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A survey item states most staff agree the new policy is fair, then asks for opinion

options.text: The item is neutral because it reports a fact
The item is leading because it suggests the desired answer
The item improves response rates by guiding respondents
The item only affects reliability, not responses

questions.explanation: Leading wording pushes respondents toward a particular answer, distorting measurement. Neutral phrasing avoids this bias.
questions.hint: Does the wording push an answer?

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A satisfaction scale uses labels strongly disagree to strongly agree with a middle point

options.text: A middle option is never appropriate
A middle option always improves data quality
A middle option allows neutral responses but may attract fence sitters
A middle option removes the need for clear labels

questions.explanation: A midpoint permits genuine neutrality but can be overused by respondents avoiding commitment. Design should match the construct.
questions.hint: Consider both benefits and risks of a midpoint.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Satisfaction with pay is asked before satisfaction with overall job

options.text: Order effects are the same as fatigue
Question order never affects responses
Only demographic questions cause order effects
Earlier pay questions may anchor later overall ratings

questions.explanation: Earlier questions can prime or anchor responses to later ones, biasing measurement. Randomising order or careful sequencing reduces this.
questions.hint: What might carry over from earlier items?

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A draft survey is given to a small group before full rollout

options.text: Pretesting replaces the need for a large sample
Pretesting reveals confusing wording and timing issues
Pretesting is only for qualitative interviews
Pretesting guarantees the final survey is valid

questions.explanation: A pilot or pretest uncovers problems with wording, flow, and timing before full deployment. It improves but does not guarantee validity.
questions.hint: What can a small trial catch?

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Name a source of sampling error
questions.stem: Random selection from the staff list still leaves some error

options.text: Sampling error stems from biased questions
Sampling error stems from data entry mistakes
Sampling error stems from using a subset of the population
Sampling error stems from nonresponse only

questions.explanation: Even with perfect random selection, sampling error arises from observing a subset rather than the full population. Other errors are separate.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: The staff list excludes recently hired contractors

options.text: This creates no error if contractors are few
This creates sampling error only
This creates measurement error only
This creates coverage error in the sampling frame

questions.explanation: When the frame omits part of the target population, coverage error results regardless of how well sampling proceeds within the frame.
questions.hint: Who is missing from the list?

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A report uses one scale that measures only burnout

options.text: A single-construct instrument is always shorter
A single-construct instrument targets one defined concept
A single-construct instrument cannot be reliable
A single-construct instrument measures everything related

questions.explanation: A single-construct instrument is designed to measure one concept cleanly, improving interpretability. Length is a separate design choice.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Burnout is defined as a score of at least 27 on a 0 to 30 scale; a worker scores 29

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a confound in a comparison
questions.stem: The report compares two teams that also differ in tenure and workload

options.text: Confounds are the same as outcomes
Only random factors can confound a comparison
Tenure and workload may confound the team comparison
Confounds do not matter in observational reports

questions.explanation: Variables that differ alongside the predictor and affect the outcome can confound the comparison. Observational designs require careful control.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Experts review whether survey items cover all aspects of burnout

options.text: Expert review is only for qualitative tools
Expert review proves the scale is reliable
Expert review establishes criterion validity
Expert review of item coverage supports content validity

questions.explanation: Content validity is supported when items adequately represent the full domain of the construct. Expert judgment is a common method.
questions.hint: Do the items cover the domain?

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Refine a vague topic into a question

options.text: Study how staff communicate every day
options.misconception: gives a directive, not a question

options.text: Communication matters for productivity
options.misconception: states a claim, not a question

questions.explanation: A research question specifies variables and a relationship to test. Option A names a predictor, outcome, and population, making it testable.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS

options.text: Absenteeism is lower in some offices
Flexible hours and absenteeism are related

questions.explanation: A hypothesis predicts a specific direction of effect between variables. Option A does this; the others restate the question or stay vague.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A manager claims the new policy improves everything for everyone

options.text: The policy always improves everything for everyone forever
The policy improves reported satisfaction for surveyed staff this quarter
The policy is good and should be adopted everywhere
The policy works because managers believe in it

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS

options.text: Engagement is being present and doing your job
Engagement is how much staff care about their work
Engagement is the average score on a five-item Likert scale administered monthly
Engagement is whatever managers think it is

questions.explanation: An operational definition specifies the measurement rule, instrument, and frequency. The other options describe concepts without a measurable rule.

Error rate is independent and break length is dependent
Both are independent variables
Break length is independent and error rate is dependent

Increase the margin of error to reduce sampling error
Reduce the number of strata to reduce sampling error
Increase the sample size to reduce sampling error

questions.explanation: Reminders and assurances of anonymity are standard ways to improve response rates without compromising ethics. Other tactics harm participation or ethics.

questions.stem: A report must ensure each department is represented proportionally

options.text: Use convenience sampling at one department
Use cluster sampling with department as cluster
Use stratified sampling with department as stratum
Use simple random sampling and hope for balance

questions.explanation: Stratified sampling guarantees representation of each department by sampling within strata. Cluster sampling selects whole groups instead.

questions.stem: A report must survey staff across many small remote branches cheaply

Use stratified sampling of individuals in every branch
Use census of all staff regardless of cost
Use cluster sampling by selecting whole branches

questions.topic: Margin of error and sample size
questions.learningObjective: Plan sample size for a target margin
questions.stem: To reach a 2.5 percent margin of error a report needs roughly 1600 respondents
questions.explanation: A 2.5 percent margin requires about 1600 respondents since one over square root of 1600 equals 0.025. Larger samples yield tighter margins.
questions.hint: Square the inverse of the margin.

questions.stem: A satisfaction scale tops out and cannot show further gains

options.text: Remove the top option to force variation
Increase the sample size to fix the ceiling
Use a scale with a higher ceiling or more levels
Accept the ceiling as unavoidable

questions.explanation: Extending the scale range or adding levels restores sensitivity to high performers. Sample size changes precision, not range.

questions.stem: A report justifies its sample size by the margin of error alone

options.text: Subgroup analysis never needs larger samples
Margin of error is sufficient for any report
Power is only for experiments, not surveys
Margin alone ignores power and subgroup precision needs

questions.explanation: Sample size planning should consider margins, power for planned comparisons, and precision for subgroups. Relying on one criterion is incomplete.

questions.stem: The employee list used as the frame is two years old

options.text: Keep the old frame to maintain consistency
Refresh the frame to reduce coverage error
Replace the frame with a convenience sample
Ignore turnover because it is small
